in_text_mentions: Return (TAPVR) (OMIM:%106700) is one type of cyanotic Congenital Heart Defects (CHD), in which none of the pulmonary veins connect to the left atrium and are malpositioned to the systemic venous circulation [1] (Figure 1A, 1B). TAPVR characterized by cardiac function deterioration including cyanosis, pulmonary hypertension, dyspnea, pulmonary edema, congestive heart failure affects 1 in 15,000 live births and 48.8% of them will die without surgery before the age of 1 [2]. Although TAPVR generally presents significant fatality rate, the pathogenesis is still vague and become hot research spot.

panels.rationale: Fetal (34-week) motion-corrected slice-to-volume MRI segmentation (posterior rightward projection) from a patient with prenatal TAPVD. The rendering directly demonstrates the disease anatomy: a pulmonary venous confluence (C) draining via an ascending/supracardiac vertical vein (asterisk) coursing between the right main bronchus (white mesh) and right pulmonary artery into the innominate vein/SVC, i.e., supracardiac TAPVR. The inset single-shot fast spin echo MRI shows heterogeneous lung parenchyma with small cystic areas (suspected pulmonary lymphangiectasia). This is patient-derived radiology rather than a schematic/diagram, so it is included; disease attribution is strongly supported by the caption and the TAPVD-focused article title. findings.evidence: In-text: 'a dilated right atrium and ventricle'; enlarged right atrium visible on the bicaval view (orange arrow)

panels.rationale: Single-panel preoperative transthoracic echocardiogram (bicaval view with color Doppler) from a real human patient. Caption and in-text tie the image to the article's disease focus: superior sinus venosus ASD with partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (PAPVD) opening into the right atrium, with dilated right atrium/ventricle and a left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs 2.3) — the anomalous-return physiology captured by the configured TAPVR vocabulary (article primary_disease_key total_anomalous_pulmonary_venous_return; prior triage: keep). Colored arrows mark SVC (green), right atrium (orange), interatrial septum (white) and ASD (yellow). The visibly enlarged right atrium plus in-text chamber dilatation support right-heart dilatation; the ASD shunt is left-to-right, so it is recorded as a proposed finding rather than the right-to-left shunt key. No ethnicity, age, or skin assessment applies. Confidence reflects the partial (rather than total) anomalous venous drainage in this case. [raw subtype: partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (PAPVD) with superior sinus venosus ASD]

CT or magnetic resonance imaging remains the mainstay imaging modality to diagnose PAPVD. It allows visualization of the pulmonary venous drainage anatomy and other associated abnormalities. panels.rationale: Real human-patient preoperative echocardiogram (bicaval view) from a case mapped to the configured anomalous-pulmonary-venous-return disease. The panel shows the atrial septal defect with right-heart volume overload; the in-text explicitly states 'a dilated right atrium and ventricle' with a left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs 2.3), supporting the right-heart-dilatation finding. Transparency note: the report is specifically a superior sinus venosus ASD with PARTIAL anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (PAPVD) opening into the right atrium, i.e. a partial rather than total connection, and its left-to-right shunt physiology is more typical of PAPVD than of classic cyanotic TAPVR; the bicaval view also does not by itself define a TAPVR anatomic subtype (subtype set null) and no diagnostic arrows/labels are present (only machine overlays). Included per the article's configured primary disease key and prior caption triage, with confidence tempered by the partial-versus-total distinction.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Genuine 3D volume-rendered CT of the neonate with TAPVR (disease-focused title), showing the common atrium with a right-sided juxtaposed atrial appendage. It is a real patient CT image and part of the preoperative TAPVR complex, but the highlighted finding (juxtaposed atrial appendage) is associated anatomy rather than the pulmonary venous anomaly itself, so attribution to TAPVR is contextual and confidence is moderate. No TAPVR vocabulary finding is directly shown, so it is placed in proposed_findings. B: Contrast-enhanced coronal CT of the same neonate with TAPVR showing bilateral SVC inserting into the common atrium and a large ductus arteriosus. It is a real patient CT image in the TAPVR preoperative workup; the large DA is the lesion banded for excessive pulmonary blood flow (in-text), tying it to TAPVR physiology, but the visible systemic-venous/ductal anatomy is not itself the pulmonary venous anomaly, so no TAPVR vocabulary...

in_text_mentions: heart appeared in poor condition; atrial and ventricular tachycardia very easily developed whenever the heart was touched. We noted the pulmonary artery located deeply behind the common atrium (Fig. 2). This made placing a Blalock-Taussig shunt without cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) hazardous and bilateral pulmonary artery banding difficult. Therefore, we undertook DA banding with a part of a 3-mm expanded polytetrafluoroethylene artificial graft. The banding circumference was 16 mm, which was determined to ensure a systemic oxygen saturation of around 80% and a partial arterial oxygen pressure

in_text_mentions: A 2.5‐month‐old male infant, weighing 4.5 kg, presented with moderate dyspnea, intercostal and subcostal retractions, and central cyanosis exacerbated by crying. Oxygen saturation was 60% on room air. Physical examination revealed fine crackles and mild expiratory wheezing, a 2/4 systolic murmur, a palpable but nonvisible apex beat, and mild hepatomegaly (2 cm below the costal margin). The anterior fontanelle was open and bulging. Chest radiography demonstrated mild bilateral pulmonary infiltrates (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: further investigation, an electrocardiogram (ECG) demonstrated sinus tachycardia with no evidence of ventricular hypertrophy or T wave changes. Arterial blood gas (ABG) was consistent with respiratory acidosis. Afterwards, an echocardiography was performed which showed dilated inferior vena cava (IVC) with flow reversal, dilated right atrium, stretched PFO (right to left shunt), and moderate tricuspid regurgitation with maximum gradient of 77 mmHg. There was moderate pulmonic insufficiency, dilated main pulmonary artery, grossly dilated right ventricle, and squashed left ventricle (Figure 2).
